title: The Great Sphinx of Giza
originLocation: Giza Plateau, Lower Egypt
medium: Monolithic carved nummulitic limestone bedrock with masonry repairs
creator: Royal sculptors of Pharaoh Khafre
repository: In situ, Giza Necropolis, Egypt
anatomy: recumbent leonine body with outstretched forepaws
human pharaonic head wearing pleated nemes headdress
brow-mounted royal cobra uraeus (now fragmentary)
curled feline tail wrapped along the right haunch
description: Excavated directly from the living limestone bedrock of the Giza Plateau beside Khafre's valley causeway, this 73-meter colossus is the oldest known monumental sculpture of Ancient Egypt. Fusing the intellectual sovereignty of the reigning pharaoh with the solar might of a couchant lion, it came to be venerated in the New Kingdom as Hor-em-akhet ('Horus in the Horizon'), eternal sentinel of the western necropolis.

title: Colossal Granite Sphinx of Pharaoh Hatshepsut
originLocation: Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari, Western Thebes
medium: Carved and painted Aswan red granite
creator: Royal Theban sculptors under Senenmut
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (31.3.166)
anatomy: muscular couchant lion body weighing over seven tons
female ruler's idealized face framed by a thick leonine mane and nemes
ceremonial false pharaonic beard and uraeus
taut feline forelimbs extended along a rectangular plinth
description: One of at least six monumental red granite sphinxes that lined the lower courtyard processional way of Hatshepsut's terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari, this sculpture casts the female pharaoh with the traditional royal beard and nemes headcloth of kingship. Smashed and buried in quarry pits during Thutmose III's posthumous proscription of her monuments, its reassembled granite fragments preserve subtle yellow and blue pigments accentuating her divine leonine transformation.

title: Granite Maned Sphinx of Kushite Pharaoh Taharqa
originLocation: Temple T at Kawa (Gematon), Upper Nubia, Sudan
medium: Carved gray-pink speckled granite
creator: Kushite royal workshop at Kawa
repository: British Museum, London (EA 1770)
anatomy: archaic Middle Kingdom-inspired enveloping lion mane and lion ears
distinctive Kushite portrait visage with broad cheekbones
double uraeus cobras signifying rule over Kush and Egypt
compact recumbent feline torso inscribed with Taharqa's cartouche
description: Excavated from the sandy sanctuary of Temple T at Kawa in Sudan, this compact granite sphinx merges archaizing Egyptian Middle Kingdom leonine conventions—reviving the heavy ruffed mane of Amenemhat III—with the unmistakable physiognomy and double-cobra regalia of the Nubian king Taharqa. Across its chest, a crisp hieroglyphic cartouche proclaims Taharqa beloved of Amun, embodying the dual kingship of Napata and Thebes.

title: Avenue of Ram-Headed Sphinxes (Criosphinxes) at Karnak
originLocation: First Pylon Approach, Precinct of Amun-Ra, Karnak, Luxor
medium: Carved sandstone colossi on stone pedestals
creator: Royal builders of Pharaoh Ramesses II (later usurped by Pinudjem I)
repository: In situ, Karnak Temple Complex, Luxor, Egypt
anatomy: downward-curving horns of the sacred Ovis platyura ram
recumbent leonine body flanking the sacred quay avenue
osiride figure of the pharaoh sheltered beneath each ram's chin
description: Lining the ceremonial dromos linking the Nile harbor quay to the First Pylon of Karnak, forty sandstone criosphinxes fuse the virile curled-horn ram of Amun-Ra with the solar strength of a couchant lion. Between its forepaws, each hybrid guardian cradles a diminutive mummiform effigy of the king, visually enacting divine protection over the monarch along the sacred bark procession route.

title: The Narmer Palette with Intertwined Serpopards
originLocation: Main Deposit, Temple of Horus at Hierakonpolis (Nekhen)
medium: Carved green-gray siltstone ceremonial palette
creator: Unknown royal master sculptor of King Narmer
repository: Egyptian Museum, Cairo (CG 14716 / JE 32169)
anatomy: lithe leopardess quadruped torso and clawed paws
impossibly elongated serpentine neck looping in symmetry
snarling feline head tethered by bearded attendants
description: Dominating the obverse center of this 64-centimeter siltstone ceremonial shield-palette, two confronted serpopards entwine their sinuous, serpent-like necks to frame the circular recess used for grinding malachite eye paint. Adapted from Uruk Mesopotamian glyptic motifs during Egypt's state formation, the tethering of these untamed feline-serpent hybrids symbolizes King Narmer's forcible unification of Upper and Lower Egypt into cosmic order (Maat).

title: The Two Dogs Palette ('Oxford Palette') with Serpopards and Winged Griffin
originLocation: Main Deposit, Hierakonpolis (Nekhen), Upper Egypt
medium: Low-relief carved mudstone cosmetic palette
creator: Unknown Predynastic Naqada III sculptor
repository: Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford (AN1896-1908.E.3924)
anatomy: serpopards licking a fallen gazelle around the pigment saucer
raptor-headed feline griffin sprouting comb-like dorsal wings
jackal-headed flute player charming chaotic desert fauna
description: Framed by two heraldic African wild dogs whose sculpted heads crown the slab, this Predynastic mudstone palette teems with real and supernatural creatures of the untamed desert margin (deshret). Alongside paired long-necked serpopards on the obverse, the reverse preserves one of world art's earliest winged griffins—a slender feline with falcon beak and stiff, comb-patterned wings—pursuing ibexes beside a masked, flute-playing therianthrope.

title: The Weighing of the Heart with Ammit, Book of the Dead of Hunefer
originLocation: Thebes, Upper Egypt
medium: Polychrome mineral pigment and ink on papyrus
creator: Theban funerary scribe-illuminator
repository: British Museum, London (EA 9901,3)
anatomy: elongated Nilotic crocodile snout and serrated jaws
maned leonine forequarters and spotted feline torso
bulbous hippopotamus hindquarters
description: Illuminating Spell 125 for the royal scribe Hunefer, this celebrated papyrus vignette stations the composite female demoness Ammit directly beneath the balance beam where Anubis weighs Hunefer's heart against Maat's ostrich feather. Combining the three deadliest man-killing beasts known along the Nile—crocodile, lion, and hippopotamus—she waits poised to devour any sinner's heart, inflicting an irreversible 'second death' outside Osiris's realm.

title: Ammit Poised Beside Thoth, Papyrus of Ani
originLocation: Thebes, Upper Egypt
medium: Tempera pigment and black carbon ink on papyrus roll
creator: Theban workshop scribe-painter
repository: British Museum, London (EA 10470,3)
anatomy: greenish scaled crocodilian head and neck
rosette-spotted leopard-lioness chest and forelegs
heavy turquoise-tinted hippopotamus haunches
description: In the sumptuous funerary papyrus of the Theban scribe Ani, Ammit crouches alertly behind ibis-headed Thoth as he records the verdict of the psychostasia on his scribal palette. Rather than an agent of chaos, the hybrid monster functions here as an instrument of divine justice, embodying retributive annihilation should the deceased's heart prove heavier than cosmic truth.

title: The Great Tomcat of Heliopolis Slaying Apep, Tomb of Inherkha (TT359)
creature: Apep (Apophis) and Miuty (Solar Tomcat of Ra)
originLocation: Tomb of Inherkha (TT359), Deir el-Medina, Western Thebes
medium: Tempera wall painting on plastered limestone
creator: Royal necropolis painters of Deir el-Medina
repository: In situ, Tomb TT359, Deir el-Medina, Luxor
commonsFile: Ra slays Apep (tomb scene in Deir el-Medina).jpg
anatomy: undulating multi-coiled giant serpent body
spotted solar tomcat with hare-like ears wielding a bronze knife
blood streaming from severed serpentine coils beneath the sacred ished tree
description: Painted on the vaulted burial chamber wall of Inherkha, 'Foreman of the Lord of the Two Lands in the Place of Truth,' this Spell 17 vignette dramatizes the nightly cosmic battle for sunrise. Beneath the foliage of Heliopolis's sacred persea (ished) tree, Ra manifests as the Great Tomcat Miuty, pinning the primeval chaos serpent Apep with one paw while slicing its undulating throat with a curved blade.

title: Alabaster Sarcophagus of Pharaoh Seti I Inscribed with the Book of Gates
originLocation: Tomb of Seti I (KV17), Valley of the Kings, Western Thebes
medium: Translucent carved calcite (Egyptian alabaster) inlaid with Egyptian blue
creator: Royal sculptors of the Valley of the Kings
repository: Sir John Soane's Museum, London (M1)
anatomy: towering labyrinthine coils of Apep bound in chains
protective multi-coiled Mehen serpent enveloping Ra's solar barque
fire-spitting uraeus guardians flanking the twelve underworld portals
description: Hollowed from a single monolithic block of translucent white calcite discovered by Giovanni Belzoni in 1817, Seti I's sarcophagus preserves the most complete carved text and imagery of the Book of Gates. Across its finely incised registers—originally filled with copper-frit blue paste—the protective serpent Mehen shields the sun god's barque while underworld deities fetter and harpoon the colossal chaos serpent Apep so dawn may be reborn.

title: The Sacred Bennu Bird and Double-Lion Aker, Tomb of Queen Nefertari (QV66)
originLocation: Tomb of Nefertari (QV66), Valley of the Queens, Western Thebes
medium: Polychrome painted raised plaster relief on limestone
creator: Royal artisans of Deir el-Medina under Ramesses II
repository: In situ, Tomb QV66, Luxor (1904 Schiaparelli archival plate, Museo Egizio, Turin)
commonsFile: Theban region, Valley of the Queens, QV 66, Tomb of Nefertari, 1904, photo 22 of 227 - Archivio fotografico Museo Egizio, Turin E00531.jpg
anatomy: blue-gray heron plumage with twin swept-back occipital crest feathers
long wading legs and dagger-like beak of the Heliopolitan phoenix
conjoined back-to-back lions of Aker cradling the horizon sign (akhet)
description: Captured in Ernesto Schiaparelli's 1904 discovery glass-plate photograph inside Queen Nefertari's burial complex, this vivid relief pairs two cardinal cosmic creatures of Spell 17 of the Book of the Dead. On the left stands the plumed Bennu bird—the self-created avian soul (ba) of Ra and prototype of the Greek phoenix—beside the mummified bier and the double-headed lion earth-guardian Aker supporting the solar disk between Yesterday and Tomorrow.

title: Polished Green Greywacke Cult Statue of Taweret
originLocation: Temple of Karnak, Thebes (dedicated under Pabasa and Nitocris I)
medium: Highly polished dark green greywacke (schist)
creator: Saite royal temple workshop at Thebes
repository: Egyptian Museum, Cairo (CG 39194 / JE 36574)
anatomy: snarling hippopotamus head wearing a tripartite wig and horned solar crown
bipedal pregnant belly with pendulous human breasts
feline lioness limbs and paws resting on braided sa-knots of protection
broad Nilotic crocodile tail cascading down the spine
description: Carved with mirror-like Saite polish from dense green greywacke and discovered intact inside a limestone naos at Karnak, this 96-centimeter cult figure embodies Egypt's foremost domestic protector of childbirth and mothers. By uniting the maternal ferocity of a female hippopotamus with leonine claws and a dorsal crocodile hide while resting her paws on magical sa-amulets, Taweret turned fearsome riverine predators into an invincible apotropaic shield.

title: Middle Kingdom Curved Ivory Apotropaic Wand ('Magic Knife')
creature: Procession of Apotropaic Monsters (Griffin, Serpopard, and Taweret)
originLocation: Middle or Upper Egypt (likely Lisht or Thebes)
medium: Split and incised hippopotamus canine tusk ivory
creator: Unknown Middle Kingdom ritual ivory carver
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (30.8.218)
anatomy: falcon-headed feline griffin with human head emerging between dorsal wings
long-necked serpopard biting a serpent
knife-wielding bipedal hippopotamus demoness and lion-frog genii
description: Fashioned from the curved lower canine tusk of a hippopotamus—Taweret's own sacred animal—this apotropaic wand was drawn in protective circles around birthing beds and infants to repel nocturnal ghosts and venomous creatures. Incised along its gleaming surface marches a fierce militia of solar genii ('fighters'), including a human-crested winged griffin, a snake-devouring serpopard, and knife-bearing leonine and hippopotamus guardians.

title: Ceremonial Parade Axe of Pharaoh Ahmose I with Aegean-Egyptian Griffin
originLocation: Tomb of Queen Ahhotep I, Dra' Abu el-Naga, Western Thebes
medium: Copper blade overlaid with sheet gold, electrum, lapis lazuli, carnelian, and turquoise on cedarwood haft
creator: Royal Theban goldsmiths of Ahmose I
repository: Luxor Museum, Luxor (formerly Egyptian Museum, Cairo, CG 52645)
commonsFile: Ceremonial axe of Ahmose I (both sides).jpg
anatomy: hooked eagle beak with curled spiral neck locks of Minoan inspiration
notched crest plumes and swept, polychrome-inlaid wings
couchant leonine body paired with a human-headed Heh sphinx above
description: Recovered from the gilded coffin of Queen Ahhotep at Thebes, this jewel-inlaid ceremonial battle-axe celebrates Pharaoh Ahmose I's expulsion of the Hyksos and reunification of Egypt. Below scenes of the king smiting an enemy and a sphinx offering a severed head, an exquisite cloisonné-inlaid griffin—labeled 'beloved of Montu'—fuses Minoan-Aegean spiral plumes with Egyptian royal war symbolism.

title: Phoenician-Egyptianizing Openwork Ivory Plaque of a Crowned Winged Sphinx
originLocation: Fort Shalmaneser, Nimrud (carved in a Phoenician coastal workshop using African elephant ivory)
medium: Openwork carved elephant ivory (originally gilded and inlaid)
creator: Phoenician master ivory carver trained in Egyptian royal iconography
repository: Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland (1968.45)
commonsFile: Winged Sphinx, Phoenician, Iraq, Nimrud, ivory - Cleveland Museum of Art - DSC08104.JPG
anatomy: youthful pharaonic profile crowned with the Egyptian pschent (double crown)
broad usekh collar and royal uraeus apron hanging between striding forelegs
sickle-curved feathered wings framing lotus and papyrus thickets
description: Carved in delicate à jour openwork from imported African elephant tusk to adorn aristocratic palace furniture, this plaque illustrates the prestigious diffusion of Egyptian hybrid royal imagery across the Iron Age eastern Mediterranean. Striding gracefully amid papyrus umbels, the sphinx wears the pharaonic double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt and a ceremonial apron while unfurling sweeping Levantine falcon wings.

title: Pantheistic Inlaid Bronze Figure of Bes (Hor-Asha-Khet)
originLocation: Egypt (reportedly Lower Egypt)
medium: Solid-cast bronze inlaid with gold, electrum, silver, and black copper alloy
creator: Egyptian temple metallurgist
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (29.2.3)
commonsFile: Bes-image of the god Hor-Asha-Khet MET DP139129.jpg
anatomy: grotesque dwarf-lion face of Bes surrounded by protruding animal protomes
four outstretched falcon wings and feathered hawk tail
human torso covered in inlaid cosmic eyes and jackal-headed feet trampling serpents
oval plinth encircled by an ouroboros enclosing noxious beasts
description: Cast in precious-metal-inlaid bronze during the first millennium BCE, this theologically dense statuette transforms the household dwarf-lion protector Bes into a cosmic pantheistic supreme being encompassing all divine powers (heka). Sprouting multiple animal heads, four falcon wings, and eyes across its skin while crushing scorpions and snakes inside an ouroboros ring, the hybrid deity rendered the invisible totality of the solar creator visibly invincible against chaos.

title: The Metternich Stela (Magical Cippus of Horus Crowned by Bes)
creature: Apotropaic Bes, Winged Pantheistic Spirits, and Noxious Beasts
originLocation: Heliopolis (later relocated to Alexandria; commissioned by the priest Esatum)
dateDisplay: Reign of Nectanebo II, c. 360–343 BCE
medium: Finely incised dark gray-green greywacke
creator: Royal Heliopolitan lapidary workshop under Nectanebo II
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (50.85)
anatomy: ferocious grimacing mask of lion-maned Bes surmounting the central relief
child Horus standing atop twin crocodiles clutching serpents, scorpions, a lion, and an oryx
miniature registers of winged composite genii, Taweret, and solar barques
description: The largest and most masterfully carved Egyptian healing cippus ever discovered, the Metternich Stela operated as an active ritual machine: water poured over its dense spell inscriptions and apotropaic figures was collected in a basin and drunk to cure scorpion stings and snakebites. Above the young Horus trampling crocodiles and grasping desert predators in his fists looms the frontal, tongue-baring mask of the dwarf-lion daemon Bes, commanding venomous monsters to yield.

title: Three-Headed, Four-Armed Lion God Apedemak at the Lion Temple of Naqa
creature: Polymorphic Apedemak (Kushite Lion-Serpent War and Fertility God)
originLocation: Exterior West Pylon/Rear Wall, Lion Temple at Naqa, Butana Steppe, Sudan
dateDisplay: Reign of King Natakamani and Kandake Amanitore, c. 1–20 CE
medium: Carved Nubian sandstone architectural relief
creator: Royal Meroitic sculptors of Natakamani and Amanitore
repository: In situ, Archaeological Site of Naqa, River Nile State, Sudan
anatomy: three roaring leonine heads facing left, front, and right beneath a triple hemhem crown
muscular human torso sprouting four outstretched arms making mudra-like gestures
royal Meroitic sash and kilt
description: Carved onto the sandstone rear wall of the Lion Temple at Naqa—an indigenous Kushite sanctuary deep in Sudan's Butana steppe—this extraordinary relief portrays the Meroitic state deity Apedemak with three lion heads and four human arms facing King Natakamani and Queen Amanitore. Scholars note that its multi-headed, four-armed iconography likely reflects direct Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade contacts between Meroitic Kush and early historic South Asia, fused seamlessly with Nubian leonine theology.

title: Meroitic Criosphinx Processional Way at the Temple of Amun, Naqa
creature: Nubian Criosphinx (Sacred Ram-Sphinx of Napatan-Meroitic Amun)
originLocation: Temple of Amun (Temple 200), Naqa, Sudan
medium: Carved ferruginous Nubian sandstone
creator: Meroitic royal workshop at Naqa
repository: In situ, Temple of Amun, Naqa, Sudan
anatomy: curled fleece horns hugging the cheeks of the sacred Nubian ram
couchant leonine body carved from warm desert sandstone
paired symmetrical alignment guarding the desert sanctuary portal
description: Stretching beyond the Roman-influenced Kiosk at Naqa, twelve monolithic sandstone ram-sphinxes flank the ceremonial approach to the Meroitic Temple of Amun. Continuing a thousand-year Kushite tradition rooted at Jebel Barkal and Kawa, these desert criosphinxes embody Amani (Amun) in his distinctly Nubian criomorphic manifestation as lord of royal legitimacy and life-giving savanna rains.

title: The Nile Mosaic of Palestrina Depicting the Legendary Beasts of Aethiopia
creature: Ethiopian Onocentaur, Giant Rock Python, and Frontier Hybrids
originLocation: Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, Praeneste (Palestrina), after an Alexandrian royal painting
medium: Polychrome opus vermiculatum limestone and glass-paste tesserae mosaic
creator: Alexandrian master mosaicists working in Italy (atelier of Demetrios the Topographer tradition)
repository: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Palestrina, Italy
anatomy: upper-register crags of Nubia and Ethiopia populated by Greek-labeled marvels
human-headed equine-asinine onocentaur and spotted hyena-lion krokottas
colossal rock-dwelling serpent coiling beside Kushite hunters
description: Spanning nearly six meters across an apsidal grotto pavement, the Nile Mosaic charts the river's entire course from Hellenistic temples in the Egyptian Delta up to its mythic headwaters in the highlands of Nubia and Ethiopia. In the rugged upper register, Alexandrian naturalism merges seamlessly with ancient teratology as Kushite archers hunt beside exotic fauna and Greek-inscribed frontier marvels—including the human-faced onocentaur, the krokottas, and giant bird-snatching pythons.

title: Gondarine Illuminated Vellum Folio: Saint George (Qeddus Giyorgis) Slaying the Dragon
originLocation: Northern Ethiopian Highlands (preserved in Axum, Tigray)
medium: Mineral and organic tempera pigments on prepared goat-skin vellum (branna)
creator: Ethiopian Orthodox monastic scribe-illuminator
repository: Treasury of the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion, Axum, Ethiopia
commonsFile: Ethiopian St. George And The Dragon - Detail (2848032429).jpg
anatomy: striated green-and-ochre serpentine body knotted at the bottom margin
wolf-like fanged snout and horned crest
spear-pierced jaws beneath the maiden Birhanawit sheltering in a tree
description: Painted in radiant vermilion, orpiment yellow, and malachite green on heavy parchment during Ethiopia's Second Gondarine style, this manuscript miniature celebrates Qeddus Giyorgis—patron warrior-saint of Ethiopia—rescuing the maiden Birhanawit perched high in a sycamore tree. In Ethiopian highland tradition, the defeated dragon resonates directly with indigenous legends of Wainaba / Arwe, the primordial tribute-demanding python king overthrown at Axum's dawn.

title: Winged Cherubim Sanctuary Ceiling of Debre Berhan Selassie
originLocation: Church of Debre Berhan Selassie ('Trinity at the Mount of Light'), Gondar, Ethiopia
dateDisplay: Founded c. 1694 CE (ceiling murals painted late 17th–early 19th century, pre-1825)
medium: Glue-tempera pigment on primed cotton cloth mounted over juniper wood ceiling beams
creator: Gondarine liturgical workshop (traditionally attributed to Haile Meskel's school)
repository: In situ, Debre Berhan Selassie Church, Gondar, Ethiopia
commonsFile: Ceiling Angels, Church of Debra Berhan Selassie (2423987689).jpg
anatomy: disembodied haloed angelic heads with immense almond-shaped watchful eyes
interlocking crimson, black, and ochre feathered wings replacing corporeal limbs
rhythmic directional gazes shifting left, right, and center across the firmament
description: Spanning the flat timbered ceiling of Debre Berhan Selassie in the royal capital of Gondar, more than eighty bodiless winged cherubim gaze down in hypnotic rows symbolizing the omniscient heavenly host surrounding the tabot (Ark). Rendered strictly as luminous, wide-eyed faces flanked by patterned red-and-black wings, these celestial guardians gained legendary renown in Ethiopian history when a miraculous swarm of bees reportedly defended the church from Mahdist destruction in 1888.

title: Royal Benin Cast Brass Figure of the Divine Oba with Mudfish Legs
originLocation: Royal Palace, Benin City (Edo State, southern Nigeria)
medium: Lost-wax (cire perdue) cast copper alloy (brass)
creator: Royal Guild of Brass Casters (Igun Eronmwon), Benin City
repository: Brooklyn Museum, New York (56.6.72)
commonsFile: Brooklyn Museum 56.6.72 Human Figure with Mudfish legs.jpg
anatomy: regal human torso wearing coral-bead collar (odigba) and netted tunic
twin undulating, whiskered mudfish (Clarias) replacing the ruler's legs
amphibious gill plates and segmented caudal fins curving outward
description: Cast by the hereditary royal brass-casters' guild of Benin City, this sacred figure portrays the divine Edo monarch (Oba) with his lower limbs transformed into living, undulating West African mudfish—creatures revered for surviving both underwater and across dry riverbeds. The hybrid iconography commemorates the mythical fourteenth-century Oba Ohen and proclaims the king's liminal sovereignty over both the terrestrial realm and the fathomless oceanic palace of Olokun, god of wealth and primordial waters.

title: Royal Benin Court Brass Leopard Aquamanile (Ekpen)
creature: Ekpen (Supernatural King of the Forest and Alter Ego of the Oba)
localName: Ekpen ('Leopard of the Bush' / Counterpart to Ekpen n'Owa)
originLocation: Royal Palace, Benin City (Edo State, southern Nigeria)
medium: Lost-wax cast brass with punched ring-dot pelt engraving
creator: Royal Guild of Brass Casters (Igun Eronmwon), Benin City
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (1978.412.321)
anatomy: taut, tubular feline torso covered in stippled double-circle spots
upright leaf-shaped ears and bared interlocking fangs
hinged cranial lid and nostril spout for pouring consecrated water
arching tail curved rigidly forward over the spine
description: Used during royal Igue purification rites to pour consecrated water over the Oba's hands at ancestral palace altars, this cast-brass aquamanile embodies the supernatural bush leopard (Ekpen), ordained by the creator Osanobua as sovereign of the wild forest just as the Oba ('Leopard of the Home') rules humankind. Its stylized vertical ears, geometric double-ring rosettes, and bared fangs visualize the terrifying occult authority (ase) by which the divine king strikes swiftly and without error.

title: Bamana Ci Wara (Chiwara) Sacred Antelope-Aardvark Crest Headdress
creature: Ci Wara ('Farming Wild Beast' — Divine Offspring of Sky and Cobra)
localName: Ci Wara Kun (Bamana: 'Head of the Farming Beast')
originLocation: Ségou or Beledougou region, Mali
medium: Carved wood, brass tacks, metal strips, and plant fiber
creator: Bamana master blacksmith-sculptor (numu)
repository: Brooklyn Museum, New York (77.245.1)
commonsFile: Brooklyn Museum 77.245.1 Dance Headdress Ci-wara Kun.jpg
anatomy: soaring lyre-curved horns of the roan antelope symbolizing sprouting millet
openwork zigzag mane tracing the solar path across the sky
low-slung burrowing body and tapering snout of the aardvark and scaly pangolin
description: Carved by a Bamana numu (blacksmith-sculptor) and lashed atop a woven basketry cap over a flowing raffia costume, this crest headdress honors Ci Wara—the mythical half-mortal, half-beast born from the primordial goddess Mousso Koroni and a cobra spirit who first taught humanity agriculture with his claws and digging stick. Combining upward-soaring roan antelope horns (sun and sky) with the earth-burrowing snout and back of an aardvark and pangolin (soil and water), male and female Ci Wara pairs danced across Mali's fields to bless tireless cultivators.

title: Senufo Kponyugo ('Firespitter') Composite Poro Society Helmet Mask
originLocation: Northern Côte d'Ivoire (Korhogo region)
medium: Monoxylous carved hardwood
creator: Senufo master woodcarver (kulebele)
repository: Brooklyn Museum, New York (1990.220)
commonsFile: Brooklyn Museum 1990.220 Firespitter Helmet Mask Kponyugo.jpg
anatomy: gaping crocodile-hyena jaws bristling with carved teeth
upturned warthog tusks jutting from the upper snout
sweeping bushbuck antelope horns framing the domed cranium
primordial chameleon and hornbill perched atop the helmet
description: Worn horizontally over the masquerader's head during Poro men's initiation funerals and nocturnal anti-witchcraft rites, the Kponyugo synthesizes the deadliest and most magically potent animals of the West African savanna into a single terrifying chimera. Combining hyena-crocodile jaws, warthog tusks, antelope horns, and a cranial chameleon—first creature to tread the newly formed earth in Senufo cosmology—these masks earned the colonial sobriquet 'firespitters' because performers blew glowing embers and burning tinder through their fanged maws into the night.

title: Nalu-Baga Sacred Rainbow-Python Crest Mask (Mbanchong / Bansonyi)
civilization: Nalu and Baga Peoples (Upper Guinea Coast)
originLocation: Coastal mangrove estuaries of Guinea
medium: Carved wood with polychrome red, white, and black earth pigments
creator: Nalu-Baga ritual sculptor
repository: Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac (displayed at Pavillon des Sessions, Palais du Louvre, Paris)
commonsFile: Guinea, nalu, parte superiore di una maschera mbanchong a forma di serpente, xix-inizio xx sec. 01.JPG
anatomy: towering vertical undulating serpent column painted with geometric chevrons
horned, narrow-snouted python head poised to strike from above
hollowed basal socket fitted over an initiate dancer's shoulders
description: Rising up to two meters vertically above a raffia-shrouded dancer during generational initiation cycles along Guinea's mangrove coast, this polychrome crest carving embodies the formidable water-and-rainbow python spirit revered by Nalu and Baga communities as Mbanchong, Bansonyi, or Ninkinanka. As paired serpent towers swayed and darted above village rooftops like rival lineage guardians emerging from sacred forest pools, they mediated rain, fertility, and cosmic balance between riverine spirits and human society.

title: San Rock Shelter Painting of an Antelope-Hoofed Therianthrope and Dying Eland ('The Rosetta Stone Panel')
originLocation: Game Pass Shelter, Kamberg Nature Reserve, KwaZulu-Natal Drakensberg, South Africa
medium: Red/yellow iron-oxide ochre, white clay, charcoal, and eland blood binder on sandstone rock face
creator: San shaman-artist (!gi:xa)
repository: In situ, Game Pass Shelter, uKhahlamba-Drakensberg Park, South Africa
anatomy: elongated human torso wearing a kaross cloak and sprouting bristling trance hairs
cloven antelope hooves and eared eland head replacing human extremities

description: Celebrated by archaeologist David Lewis-Williams as the 'Rosetta Stone' of southern African rock art, this polychrome sandstone panel at Game Pass Shelter depicts a San medicine person physically metamorphosing into an antelope-hoofed, eared therianthrope while clutching the tail of a stumbling eland. Painted with ochre mixed with eland blood—itself a reservoir of supernatural potency (n/om)—the scene records the visionary realm of the healing trance dance, in which shamans merged with spirit elands and rain-animals to summon rain and cure affliction.
